EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe assures the equality and dignity of all 
persons as a signatory to the UN Declaration of Human Rights. It recognizes the non-violation 
and the non-alienation of these rights without discrimination as to gender, social, economic, 
racial, religious, political or economic origin. All citizens are guaranteed these fundamental rights 
under the 1990 Constitution. 
Sao Tome and Principe has included the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in its 
Constitution, has ratified the majority of conventions and international instruments to protect the 
rights of its citizens, and has signed along with all UN country members, the Millennium 
Declaration.
The elaboration of the Common Country Assessment (CCA) and the United Nations 
Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) for the Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and
Principe have been framed within a new planning and cooperation phase of the United Nations 
(UN) System and its agencies, programmes and funds1, thus responding to the demands of the 
UN Reform initiated by Secretary General, Kofi Annan, in 1997.
UNDAF Outcomes derived from the findings of six thematic groups established for the 
elaboration of the CCA. The areas prioritized were based on national priorities set forth by the 
government in relation to the mandates and missions of the agencies, programmes and funds of 
the UN System present in the country; the approved Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP) 
(2002); and progress towards the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs). 
Other factors assessed include the potential for improving the living conditions of vulnerable 
populations; and the possibilities of partnership with bilateral and multilateral donors working in 
the country.
The two strategic UNDAF thematic areas chosen for the programme cycle 2007-2011 are:
o To address access to quality basic social services including Health, Education, HIV/AIDS 
and Environment and the protection of the most vulnerable. 
o To reinforce the capacity of public institutions in order to consolidate the rule of law and 
the protection of human rights, while ensuring the continuous involvement of civil 
society.
Given the need for gender mainstreaming in all areas of intervention of the UNDAF, the UNCT 
has agreed to include gender as a cross-cutting area, having as a result:
o Integration of gender issues at all levels of future cooperation and to ensure the equality 
of women and men in political, economic and social life.

 I. Introduction
The Common Country Assessment (CCA) and the United Nations Development Assistance 
Framework (UNDAF) have become the primary tools for the United Nations programmes, funds 
and agencies to articulate a coherent common programming framework at country level. The 
CCA/UNDAF, representing both a process and a product, are part of the Secretary General’s 
Reform programme initiated in 1997 to make the UN a more effective and efficient institution.
The CCA is the common instrument of the UN system to analyze the national development 
situation and identify key development issues2. The CCA in Sao Tome and Principe was a 
collective assessment conducted throughout a period of almost 9 months that identified the causes 
of key development challenges in the country. Six theme groups working in six different areas 
were established bringing together government experts, members of the civil society as well as 
representatives of the UN system. The CCA was finalized in November 2005 and was based on 
the findings of each thematic group. 
The UNDAF is the common strategic framework for the operational activities of the UN system 
at country level. It provides a collective, coherent and integrated UN system response to national 
priorities and needs3. It derives from the analyses of the CCA and is the next step in the 
preparation of UN system country programmes of cooperation.
The UNDAF process in the Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe started with the 
strategic planning meeting in November 2005. Representatives from the government and civil 
society were invited – together with members of the UN Country Team – to actively participate in 
the formulation of the UNDAF matrix. On the basis of the short-listed areas of cooperation 
outlined in the CCA, the approved PRSP (2002), the eight Millennium Development Goals 
(MDGs) and government priorities, participants identified national development priority areas in 
which the UN system in Sao Tome and Principe, given its comparative advantage, should 
concentrate its efforts for the next 5-year cycle.
Two strategic UNDAF outcomes were jointly formulated, in addition to a cross-cutting area of 
cooperation: 
o Outcome 1: will address access to quality basic social services including Health, Education, 
HIV/AIDS, Environment and protection of the most vulnerable. 
o Outcome 2: will reinforce the capacity of public institutions in order to consolidate the rule 
of law and the protection of human rights, which ensure the continuous involvement of civil 
society.
o Cross-cutting area: a gender dimension will be integrated at all levels of future cooperation 
and to ensure visible equality of women and men in political, economic and social 
responsibilities in life.
The UNDAF matrix, including country programme outcomes and outputs, evolved through 
successive participatory process, regular meetings and revision sessions. The whole process was 
followed and coordinated by a Steering Committee composed of the heads of agencies of the UN 
system and regular UN Country Team meetings. 
The present document, a final product of this process and fruit of the UN country team’s joint 
efforts with the government, aims to be an effective instrument to address the country’s 
development challenges throughout the next UN cycle of assistance.

II. Results Section
Priority Area 1: Basic Social Services
Overview
The Millennium Declaration clearly states the commitment by heads of states and governments to 
help people reach their human potential by allowing them to lead the lives they value. This 
implies the ability to satisfy basic human needs like food and shelter, to enjoy a healthy life, as 
well as having the means for self-development and the opportunity to make choices, which come 
as a result of good education and participation in decision-making. 
Through the lenses of the Millennium Declaration, and in line with the priorities and the 
objectives defined within the 2002 Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper; the UN System in Sao 
Tome and Principe is working with the government to reinforce the capacities of its citizens to 
fulfill their potential in society. As widely recognized by all partners, unless food, nutrition, 
shelter, basic education and health care are ensured and sustained, the poverty trap in which the 
country is caught will prevail, due not only to lack of financial resources but also to the limited 
opportunities to make the right choices in life.
National Priority: human resource development and access to basic social services
The first UNDAF thematic area will address access to quality basic social services including 
Health, Education, HIV/AIDS, Environment and the protection of the most vulnerable. 
« Outcome 1: By 2011, a larger number of vulnerable populations will have access to 
quality basic social services and a healthy environment»
Corresponding to these priorities and needs, the UN System in Sao Tome and Principe has 
aligned its collective response to achieve through its programmes four targeted outcomes:
1. Increased access to quality health services by vulnerable populations 
Despite the advances achieved in the area of health, like a steady decrease of child and adolescent 
mortality and a longer life expectancy, several challenges remain. The country is facing an 
increasingly high rate of maternal mortality and the prevalence of infectious diseases including 
malaria, which despite being addressed, is still very prevalent. Malnutrition, lack of hygiene, and 
the difficulty to access health care service and medicines continue to be among the main 
morbidity factors.
In terms of the capacity of the health sector, poor infrastructure and shortage of medicines and 
medical material have led to an inadequate health care system unable to ensure basic prevention 
measures. It has also disallowed the appropriate follow up of individual patients, or the evolution 
of the health care system in general.
The elaboration of the PRSP in 2002 provided the government with a more focused approach to 
health, and put in place a Health Strategic Plan, thus updating what had been planned in 1996. 
Specific measures were introduced, for example the improvement of vaccine coverage, the 23 January 2006
7
availability of antiretroviral (ARVs) drugs, and the adoption of a 5-year Strategic Plan against
Malaria with the personal involvement by the President of the Republic. Within the ministerial 
strategic plan the authorities also validated a National Strategic Plan (NSP) to respond to 
HIV/AIDS, defined an information strategy to put in place a unique operational health system, 
and substantially increased the health allocation within the national budget from 8% in 2002 to 
19% in 2004.
Substantial efforts will need to be made to cover basic health needs, and to achieve the MDGs. 
Within the framework of the present UNDAF, while addressing the right to life and the right to 
health, the UNCT will work together to provide better access to reproductive health services to 
the general population, especially to youth and adolescents; will continue working in the 
implementation of the national plan to roll back malaria, and to keep vaccines for all antigens at 
least at a 95% coverage rate to targeted populations. Given current constraints to access essential 
medicines and health reproductive products, the UNCT will increase access to them while 
improving the technical capacity of health personnel. Moreover, prevention and advocacy 
programmes on malnutrition will be put in place to improve general awareness about health and 
nutrition (particularly for pregnant and breastfeeding women, and children under 5 years old).
2. Reinforcement of the HIV/AIDS multisectorial response within national institutions and 
civil society 
Even though the HIV/AIDS prevalence rate is still low (1% in 2001) the potential danger to 
become a major epidemic exists. A study conducted in 2000 showed that 47% of the population 
was infected by sexually transmitted diseases while condom use was estimated to be very low. 
Moreover the increasing prevalence among pregnant woman, which grew from 0.1% in 2001 to 
1.5% in 2005, illustrates the potential danger that the country might face in a few years. 
Condom distribution especially as a preventive measure against HIV infection and as a family 
planning intervention is carried out simultaneously and without coordination by public family 
planning health centers and NGOs; in addition information, education and communication 
campaigns are still weak and insufficient to sensitize the general population and promote 
behavioral change. Besides data collection, statistics and substantive studies exist in this area are 
limited.
Although the capacity to plan and monitor integrated health policies for epidemics like malaria, 
HIV/AIDS or tuberculosis is still weak in the country, the Government of Sao Tome and Principe 
has been addressing the issues of HIV/AIDS prevention and control for the last 10 years and has 
validated the HIV/AIDS National Strategic Plan (NSP) in 2003.
The UN system has been supporting the country in its efforts to strengthen and expand its 
response to the HIV/AIDS through individual agencies’ programmes. In the present UNDAF, the 
UNCT will emphasize joint initiatives and focus on three priority areas, namely (1) multisectorial 
response at national level, which includes reinforcing the technical capacity of national 
institutions, providing better access to quality voluntary counseling and testing centers, and 
ensuring quality blood screening and safe blood banks; (2) an advocacy and communication 
strategy for awareness and behavioral change, which will concentrate on providing better access 
to information and advocacy campaigns on healthy sexual behavior, and addressing stigma and 
discrimination; and (3) care and support to those infected or affected by HIV/AIDS, thus looking 
into protection of the rights of people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA), assistance and care to 
AIDS orphans as well as food security to the families affected by the virus. 
3. Access to quality basic education by the population at large is improved23 January 2006
8
The Constitution of the Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe assures the right to 
education, reflecting the responsibility of the government to respect international human rights 
conventions, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified in 1991. 
Even though the education system at large faces serious problems, the literacy rate is 83.1% for 
adults and youth above 15 years. The law provides the right to primary education and divides the 
education system in three parts: primary education, secondary education and tertiary education.
Primary education is universal, obligatory and free by law. It comprises two cycles, of four and 
two years respectively. So far, only the first cycle is ensured whereas access to the second cycle 
of 5th and 6th grades is limited and offered by very few schools. Furthermore the distance that 
students have to commute, especially to attend 4th grade and beyond, aggravates the situation. In 
this context, primary school completion has witnessed a decline throughout the last 15 years, 
from a 97% rate in 1990 to a 69.3% rate in 2002, leaving one third of the children out of school, 
and with girls being the greatest victims of faster drop-out rates. 
Secondary education is also geographically limited to large urban centers and goes from 7th to 
11
th grades. For higher education there is only one public polytechnic institution and a private 
institute that offers accounting and administrative studies. While waiting for a more sustainable 
national solution to this problem, the government has agreed to give 300 scholarships for 
education abroad, and a project to create a private university has been submitted for consideration 
in 2006.
Looking at basic and fundamental rights, and in line with International Conventions and the 
MDGs, perhaps the largest challenge in the immediate future for the Government will be to 
guarantee universal primary education to all the children of Sao Tome and Principe. Failing to 
guarantee such right will seriously jeopardize achieving universal primary education by 2015. 
The situation described above shows a contradiction between the principles of the Right to 
education largely endorsed by the government, and the economic and social reality. The resources 
allocated to the education system do not allow to respond to the increasing demand for education, 
or to improve the quality of teachers and supervisory staff in the school system, or to offer 
technical and vocational training relevant to local market needs.
In order to address these obstacles, several steps have been taken in recent years by different 
actors:
Primarily, the PRSP framework provided a general orientation to develop the schooling system, 
to address illiteracy and to enhance vocational training. It was based on a series of principles: (1) 
decentralization and commitment by all actors involved in the education process, (2) 
prioritization of primary education, (3) improvement of efficiency and quality of education, (4) 
adoption of positive discriminatory measures towards children from poor households, and (5) 
coordination between education, training and employment programmes to better prepare young 
people and adults in their professional lives. 
Secondly, in close collaboration with the donors, the National Education and Training Strategic 
Plan was introduced along with a 10-year plan for the development of the Education sector. At 
the same time, the government engaged in the 20/20 initiative and additional financial resources 
were allocated by bilateral and multilateral donors African Development Bank (ADB), World 
Bank (WB) and Portugal.23 January 2006
9
Lastly, the Government has committed itself to distribute 14% of the resources of the Programme 
of Priority Actions 2006-2008 to the education sector, and will give particular consideration to 
open a technical and professional department in the sector.
Considering people’s education as the engine to activate economic efficiency, and allowing for 
individual development to enable active participation of citizens in public life, the UN System 
fully endorses such commitment and will support education system’ reform, improved universal 
primary education that ensures girls education and advancement within the spirit of the MDGs 
and the ‘education for all’ initiative.
In the present UNDAF, basic education will continue to be reinforced by relevant UN agencies 
and bilateral donors. The UNCT will focus its intervention on improving the quality of education, 
reducing gender disparities, as well as making education accessible to the most vulnerable. 
Quality education will be improved by reinforcing teacher’s skills, reviewing the school 
curriculum, and providing books and educational material. The UNCT will work to increase 
access to basic education for women and girls thus reducing gender disparities; and access to 
knowledge and learning facilities to illiterate populations or those in most need, through 
alternative learning methods, and distance learning education using new technologies. Finally 
basic nutritional needs will also be ensured in primary schools, through school feeding 
programmes.
4. Access by the population at large to safe water and sanitation and a protected 
environment ensured
The population in Sao Tome and Principe is disproportionately distributed between two islands. 
Large urbanization has taken place especially after independence, resulting in the population 
being mainly concentrated in the capital, where the demographic growth rate is as high as 5%.
Most of the population lives without access to basic services particularly electricity, safe water, 
and appropriate sanitation. Electricity cuts are frequent in rural areas, villages and the capital. 
Water remains a major problem, as access to a clean source is difficult. Water is supplied through 
rainforest collection system, which is outdated and insufficient to respond to the growing 
demand. In terms of sanitation, there has been latrine construction in semi-urban zones and rural 
plantation areas however they are not generally used. According to the MDG report, the country 
does not have a suitable mechanism to collect and treat solid waste. Hospitals waste is an 
additional problem unsolved. 
Environmental degradation is basically due to the use of wood as fuel by poor rural families, 
wood exploitation for commercial gain, and deforestation of large areas to produce banana and 
corn. At the same time, the shoreline is also facing degradation due to indiscriminate extraction of 
sand and the release of polluted water into the ocean. On the positive side, the indicators of 
atmospheric pollution are not alarming, as there are no major industries.
Given current conditions, attention will be given to improve the habitat and its basic services. 
Currently, the population’s human, financial and infrastructural conditions do not satisfy basic 
fundamental rights to enjoy a healthy life, hence ensuring environmental sustainability by 2015, 
particularly within the MDG’s framework, may not be achieved.
Government within the PRSP aims to substantially increase access to collective water systems 
and improve the quality of water supply, in rural as well as in urban areas. In terms of sanitation, 23 January 2006
10
it proposes to increase solid waste collection in urban and semi-urban areas by 100%, and provide 
all households with sanitary facilities. It also plans to rehabilitate the old sewage systems in the 
capital and to carry out a large campaign to promote healthy practices and life styles. In addition, 
among recent actions by the public sector to address environmental constraints in line with the 
World Summit in Johannesburg in 2002, the government has established the National 
Environmental Plan for Sustainable Development (NEPSD). The NEPSD provides a strategic 
vision on how to ration and use national water and other resources and protect the environment, it 
also includes a multisectoral approach to add environmental issues within sectoral development 
plans, and a national coordination body to address environment and sustainable development.
In the following programme cycle 2007-2011 and under the UNDAF, combined agency efforts 
will help local communities and NGOs in the sustainable management of water, and to improve 
hygiene infrastructures and measures for targeted populations. The UN system will also work 
closely with national authorities to help them comply and enforce international environmental 
conventions; especially the commitments made in the Rio Convention, and it will also reinforce 
the management capacity of national environmental institutions in charge of implementing the 
NEPSD.
Priority Area 2: Good Governance and Human Rights
Overview
In order to enhance people’s human potential, the state and its organs have to create the right 
environment for human development. Under the new social contract that the government is 
engaging into with the UN System, donors, civil society and other partners, a balance must be 
established between the demands of a market economy and the social well-being of its citizens. 
At the heart of this new social contract is a human-rights based approach that includes women as 
key players in the growth and development processes of the nation.
The Republic of Sao Tome and Principe gained independence in 1975 and only engaged in a 
democratic processes in 1990, the year in which the new Constitution was adopted by a 
referendum. The country’s constitution encourages a multi-party system and free choice as sociopolitical options for the state. Freedom of religion, freedom of expression, the right to association 
and other collective and individual rights, including equal rights of all citizens without 
distinction, are guaranteed. Women are recognized with equal rights in the family, and as citizens 
with elective power, although in reality their equality is not always evident. 
The country will soon become a producer of oil. Revenues so generated may be of such a 
magnitude that the current forms of socio-economic organization will become obsolete, pushing 
the country to undertake major restructuring. If the country is to succeed in its socio-economic 
development plans, the essential links between state and human capabilities – democratic 
participation, a social contract and the rule of law – must be established now.
A central part of State reform will be to reinforce public institutions’ capacity to plan, implement 
and follow up procedures at central and local level, so as to improve service delivery and ensure a 
more transparent and efficient use of national resources. The challenge is to build an environment 
that will allow the most vulnerable to benefit from economic growth opportunities and ensure 
efficiently utilized, targeted spending on social development sectors like health and education.
To reinforce state capabilities, the UN System will help the government prioritize public 
institutional reform and establish the rule of law, optimize external assistance, promote a form of 23 January 2006
11
participative democracy, protect the rights of the most vulnerable (especially women and 
children) against abuse and all forms of discrimination, transfer power and authority to the local 
levels to prompt greater citizen participation, and reduce regional disparities by providing a safety 
net for the most vulnerable social groups.
National Priority: public institutional reform, reinforcement of national capacity and 
promotion of a policy of good governance 
The second UNDAF thematic area will reinforce the capacity of public institutions in order 
to consolidate the rule of law and to protect human rights, ensuring the continuous 
involvement of civil society.
« Outcome 2: By 2011, public institutions ensure the protection of human rights, equity 
within natural resource distribution and sustained dialogue with civil society »
Corresponding to these priorities and needs, the UN System in Sao Tome and Principe has 
aligned its collective response to achieve through its programmes three targeted outcomes:
1. Public institutions are reinforced to ensure their own reform and the transparent 
application of the law
It is important to note that the history of the Sao Tome and Principe - with its Portuguese 
colonial legacy, the late attainment of independence and the slow democratic process- did not 
provide a solid ground for sustained democracy, political stability and a strong public 
administration system. The country faces major administration inefficiency, due to the poor 
preparation and training of its staff, low salaries, limited incentives in the public administration 
system, and the absence of clear administrative procedures and systematic implementation of 
rules and regulations. 
Within the framework of the PRSP, several measures were put in place to consolidate democracy 
and the rule of law. Some of the measures included reinforcing civil servants’ capacities and legal 
structures; promoting an effective and transparent management, and reorganizing and 
modernizing the public administration and promoting a process of decentralization.
In economic terms and national resource management, the country will soon become a producer 
of oil, and this will generate a major resource influx. However, oil exploitation is expected to be 
limited in time, thus making the oil revenues only transitory. Therefore the good management of 
oil resources will be essential to make this large endowment, a catalyst for sustained development 
and of real benefit to all societies members of the country. To this end, the President of the 
Republic promulgated a law in December 2004 to establish a legal framework along with specific 
mechanisms so that oil revenues are used in a transparent and effective way. 
In the next country programme cycle and within the UNDAF framework, the UN system through 
its programmes, agencies and funds will be working in several areas:
In the area of human rights protection, and ensuring equality without discrimination, the UN 
system will continue to join forces to enhance the legal and institutional framework to protect the 
rights of the children, youth and the most vulnerable, including people living with HIV/AIDS; 23 January 2006
12
and will reinforce the capacity of institutions in charge of implementing the national strategy for 
gender equity and equality. 
In terms of institutional capacity and enhancing administration’s efficiency, the UN system will 
focus on the one hand on accelerating the state reform process in the areas of health and 
education, and on the other, on reinforcing the capacity of judiciary institutions to guarantee the 
rule of law.
In order to increase citizen’s capabilities of greater participation and choice, it will be important 
to reinforce their awareness of national priorities, and improve society’s knowledge of their civil, 
political and economic rights. To this end, efforts will be made to strengthen the capacity of the 
media to inform freely and objectively, and to improve socio-economic information management 
systems making them more transparent and available to the population at large.
The international community, including the UN system, will also work to ensure transparency of 
resource utilization, especially those coming from the oil, and will help structure the institutional 
development and management capacity of the public machinery, thus ensuring that the country 
benefits from this golden opportunity. 
2. Aid harmonization and coordination system is in place
After many years of macroeconomic instability, with a chronic deficit in the balance of payments, 
depreciation of the local currency, and repeated inflation, the country is facing large debts. The 
country joined the Highly Indebted Poor Country (HIPIC) group in 2000 and has since been 
eligible for its benefits. According to World Bank estimates the debt of the country reached USD 
361 million in 2005, one of the highest world figures if considered relatively to the Gross 
Domestic Product (GDP).
The reestablishment of dialogue with international financial institutions to address the macroeconomic issues resulted in an agreement in August 2005. A triennial Programme of Priority 
Actions 2006-2008 was funded by a public investment Plan of USD 168,7 million, 35% of which 
will be allocated to economic growth, and 26% to improve income diversification of the poor.
The balance of payments has been regularly underwritten by international Aid assistance that 
reached the level of USD 25 millions in 2004..
Two High-Level Forums on Aid Harmonization and Alignment, attended by leaders of the major 
multilateral development banks, international and bilateral organizations, and donor and recipient 
country representatives took in place in Rome in 2003 and in Paris in 2005. The results of such 
forums have been a large commitment by the international community to improve the 
management and effectiveness of aid. In the last forum in Paris, institutions and countries 
reinforced their willingness to continue increasing efforts in harmonization, alignment, and 
managing for results, paying special attention to monitoring actions and indicators to accelerate 
progress at country level. 
Along these lines, and in order to help make better use of external assistance and to better address 
increasing donor harmonization constraints, specialized UN agencies will help the government 
establish an Aid Coordination Unit.
3. Effective decentralization to redistribute the national income 
Within the context of poverty reduction, developing and implementing pro-poor decentralized 
policies and ensuring they are reinforced by appropriate mechanisms and resources will be central 23 January 2006
13
for effective decentralization and redistribution of national income. Moreover, strategic urban and 
rural planning will facilitate the decentralization process, while improving the quality of 
government services, making them more demand-driven, equitable and accessible. 
It is worth highlighting that due to continued political instability in Sao Tome and Principe , until 
the establishment of the PRSP, the main actions envisaged within the government reform 
remained stagnant, especially in the area of decentralization where the last regional and municipal 
elections took place in 1994.
Under the current UNDAF, and in order to improve decision-making processes aimed at 
impacting people’s lives at the local level, the UNCT will build capacity among community 
actors to enhance participation and local development; and at the same time, will continue 
working on reinforcing city council capacities, to enhance their ability to manage local resources 
and adapt them to local needs.
Cross-cutting area of cooperation: Gender
The UNCT proposes to keep gender issues as a cross-cutting area having as a result:
« By 2011, a gender dimension will be integrated at all levels of future cooperation to 
ensure visible equality of women and men in political, economic and social life»
Women represent at least half of the society of Sao Tome and Principe, therefore unless gender 
inequalities are addressed, and women are guaranteed equal access to social services including 
equal participation in decision-making, the success of the UNDAF will be jeopardized, as it will 
exclude 50% of the country’s population without their needs being addressed. This will not only 
have a major negative impact in the country’s development, but it will violate one of the first 
principles in the Declaration of Human Rights and the country’s Constitution.
In this context, and to ensure a gender sensitive process that will lead towards a more equal and 
participatory society, gender issues will be mainstreamed throughout the UNDAF programme 
cycle.
III. Estimated Resource Requirements 
The estimated resource allocation by the UN agencies, programmes and funds present in the 
country is approximately USD 11,5 million, in addition to at least USD 10 million that is likely to 
be mobilized. In line with MDG objective 8, such resource mobilization will require forging 
strong development partnerships.
The main actors for resource mobilization will be the agencies of the UN system present in Sao 
Tome and Principe , namely UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, WFP and WHO and other non resident 
agencies such as FAO, UNAIDS, UN Habitat; national authorities, as well as members of the 
civil society at national and local level. Efforts will also focus on expanding the traditional 
partnerships to include the private sector and other development professional groups.
At international level, efforts will be made to continue involving the traditional bilateral donors to 
the country, and to enlarge partnerships to multilateral donors like the WB, the EU, the ADB, 
International financial institutions and international NGOs. Throughout the present UNDAF 
programme cycle, particular attention will also be given to south-south cooperation.23 January 2006
14
During the whole process, round tables and theme group meetings will be organized to reinforce 
partnerships for resource mobilization. 
IV. Implementation
The two selected areas of cooperation (1) basic social services, and (2) governance and human 
rights and the cross-cutting thematic area of gender, provide a multisectorial approach for the 
implementation of the programme as well as systematic joint work/programming between 
agencies to achieve the planned UNDAF results.
The multisectorial approach will be one of the challenges of implementation, as it will require 
the identification of strategic partners, in accordance with relevant sectors and activities. At the 
same time, joint programme initiatives will be developed to ensure the right implementation of 
certain aspects of the UNDAF and to ensure impact and follow up.
In order to guarantee that programme activities are implemented effectively and efficiently, so 
that the UN optimally contributes towards the achievement of the MDGs, the UNDAF 
programme will be implemented through national execution (NEX) and to the maximum extent
possible the new modality of transfer will be applied.
The Resident Coordinator (RC), in agreement with the government and respective UN agencies, 
programmes and funds will be the responsible to put in place the appropriate mechanisms for an 
efficient implementation of the programme. 
V. Monitoring and Evaluation 
The country team with its national partners has established a Steering Committee and Thematic 
Groups to monitor and evaluate the implementation of the UNDAF, ensuring transparency of 
the UN System in its execution. 
Theme groups will be established around different areas, they will meet on a regular basis (at 
least quarterly) and will convey their conclusions and recommendations to the UNDAF Steering 
Committee. The Steering Committee will be the body in charge of analyzing the conclusions 
and recommendations of thematic groups, and will provide input and guidance to achieve the 
outcomes expected by the UN System within the joint programme cycle. 
Theme Group and Steering Committee members will be members of the board that will examine 
and approve the programmes and projects of each agency, and will participate in field visits and 
evaluation studies for the attainment of UNDAF outcomes. 
UNDAF outcomes will be monitored according to the requirements set out in the UNDAF 
guidelines. Data available through PRSP revisions, information gathered for the MDG and RC 
progress reports, as well as data from other relevant sources, international conferences and 
conventions will be used to monitor the progress of the outcome indicators against their specific 
baselines.
In addition to the mid-term and final UNDAF evaluations, the steering committee will also 
organize two thematic and impact evaluations, the first and third year of implementation. These 23 January 2006
15
will be used to examine the results obtained and to provide recommendations thus reinforcing 
the overall results and ensuring the achievement of the outcomes by the end of the cycle. At the 
end of the programme cycle, the steering committee will provide guidance and the operational 
framework for the final evaluation and will define the new axis of cooperation for the futureUnited Nations Systeme in São Tomé e Príncipe
